name: net Commands - Windows Domain Enumeration (LOTL)
description: Built-in Windows 'net' commands for domain enumeration — requires no additional tools, runs on any domain-joined Windows host. Living-off-the-land (LOTL) enumeration. Core commands: net user, net group, net accounts, net share. Always available when you have a Windows domain foothold.
source: CPTS Module 13: Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks
notes:
=== KEY NET COMMANDS FOR AD ===
  net user /domain                  → list all domain users
  net user <username> /domain       → detailed info for a specific user
  net group /domain                 → list all domain groups
  net group 'Domain Admins' /domain → list members of Domain Admins
  net group 'Enterprise Admins' /domain → EA members
  net accounts /domain              → password policy (lockout threshold!)
  net share                         → local shares
  net view /domain                  → list computers in domain
  net localgroup administrators     → local admin group members

=== WHY THESE MATTER ===
Net commands work with no imports, no executables, no PowerShell.
Ideal for:
  - Initial enumeration immediately after landing on a Windows box
  - Environments where PowerShell is restricted or monitored
  - Quick checks before deploying PowerView or SharpHound

=== GET PASSWORD POLICY FAST ===
net accounts /domain
  Account lockout threshold: 5
  Account lockout observation window: 30 minutes
  Account lockout duration: 30 minutes
This is what you need before spraying.

=== LIMITATIONS ===
  - Limited output compared to PowerView
  - No attribute-level filtering
  - Can't enumerate ACLs, trusts, or detailed user attributes
  - Use PowerView/BloodHound for deeper enumeration Also covered in: OSCP PEN-200 Chapter 21 (Active Directory Introduction and Enumeration).

defense.why_it_works: Built-in `net user/group /domain` commands enumerate domain users and groups using native Windows binaries - no tools dropped.
defense.impact: User/group enumeration using trusted built-ins that blend with admin activity.
defense.detection: [MITRE T1087.002/T1069.002] net.exe with /domain in process logs (4688); the resulting LDAP/SAMR queries to the DC.
defense.prevention: AD is readable by any authenticated user by design, so prevention is limited - focus on DETECTION (Defender for Identity, LDAP/SMB anomaly monitoring), least privilege, disabling anonymous/null sessions, and REDUCING what's exposed (remove unnecessary SPNs, descriptions with secrets, over-shared folders).
defense.evasion: net.exe is a trusted built-in, so it blends far better than PowerView/BloodHound; single targeted queries avoid bulk-read alerts.
defense.misconfiguration: Active Directory's default read ACL allows any authenticated domain user to enumerate nearly the entire directory: all user accounts, groups, SPNs, computer objects, trust relationships, and many sensitive attributes. There is no built-in 'need to know' principle on LDAP reads. BloodHound, PowerView, and ldapsearch all exploit these open default ACLs to map attack paths.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# AD default permissions — authenticated users can read:
# All user objects: sAMAccountName, userPrincipalName, memberOf, servicePrincipalName
# All computer objects: DNS names, OS versions, operating system attributes
# All group memberships, GPOs, OU structure, domain trusts

# Verify with any low-priv account:
Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties *  # returns all users + attributes
Get-ADGroup -Filter * | Get-ADGroupMember  # all group memberships
defense.secure_config:
# 1. Enable AD Recycle Bin + Protected Users group
# 2. Audit and tighten ACLs on sensitive attributes:
#    msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo, adminCount, memberOf for privileged groups

# 3. Disable SMB null sessions + restrict LDAP anonymous binds (see smb/ldap cards)

# 4. Detect enumeration via volume:
# Sysmon Event 3 (network connection) from non-DC to DC on port 389/636
# Event 4661 — access to SAM objects (high-volume; baseline first)
# Microsoft Defender for Identity: 'Account Enumeration Reconnaissance' alert

# 5. Deploy Honey accounts/objects:
# Fake high-priv account (no real access) — any LDAP query for it = attacker
# BloodHound run from non-DC = detectable via DC LDAP traffic volume

# 6. Tiered administration: Tier 0 DCs, Tier 1 servers, Tier 2 workstations
#    Each tier can only query its own tier's objects
